entities.name: Pietro Pomponazzi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pietro Pomponazzi (1462 – May 28, 1525), an influential Italian philosopher of the Renaissance, ignited a profound intellectual crisis across European universities with his heterodox interpretations of Aristotelian psychology. Born in Mantua and primarily active in the vibrant academic centers of Padua and Bologna, Pomponazzi became the most prominent exponent of Alexandrist Aristotelianism, challenging entrenched scholastic traditions regarding the nature and immortality of the human soul. His controversial work, *De immortalitate animae* (1516), directly confronted both the Thomistic synthesis of faith and reason and the Averroist doctrine of monopsychism, forcing a re-evaluation of the boundaries between philosophical inquiry and theological dogma during a period of intense religious and intellectual ferment.

Pomponazzi's central philosophical contribution lay in his rigorous analysis of Aristotle's *De Anima*, particularly his conclusion that the immortality of the individual human soul could not be proven by natural reason, but must be accepted solely as an article of faith. This position, articulated in *De immortalitate animae*, directly contradicted the prevailing Thomistic view, which held that immortality was rationally demonstrable. Teaching at the University of Padua from 1488 and later at Bologna from 1512, Pomponazzi attracted a wide following, fostering an environment where empirical observation and rational deduction were prioritized, even if they led to conclusions at odds with Church doctrine. He further explored themes of free will, fate, and the nature of miracles in *De Fato* and *De Incantationibus*, dissecting supernatural phenomena through naturalistic lenses.
